disclaimerLinks: This is not a diagnosis. Read our medical disclaimer and our privacy policy.
scope: This tool estimates your daily protein target for general health, using published intake guidelines. It is an educational screening aid, not a prescription or a diagnosis. It is for adults aged 18 and over. If you have kidney or liver disease, your protein needs must be set by your clinical team — not by a calculator.
renalStop.title: We can't give you a protein target
renalStop.body: In kidney disease, protein guidance runs in the opposite direction to general advice — national kidney guidelines recommend a reduced, closely supervised protein intake, individually set against your kidney function. A general-population number could be actively harmful here, so this tool will not produce one for you. Please ask your kidney team or a renal dietitian for your personal target. That is the right answer for you, and it is not something a public calculator can safely replace.
renalUnsure.title: Confirm your kidney function first
renalUnsure.body: You said you're not sure about your kidney function. The target below assumes healthy kidneys. If a blood test later shows reduced kidney function, this number would be too high for you — protein guidance is lowered, not raised, in kidney disease. Please treat this as provisional until a simple blood test confirms.
pregnancy.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding have their own requirement
pregnancy.body: Your target below is the published requirement for this stage, not a general fitness target — and it is a minimum, not a ceiling. Please confirm it with your midwife, obstetrician or dietitian, who can account for your individual pregnancy.
clinical.title: Confirm this with your clinician
clinical.body: You've told us about a liver condition or a recovery from serious illness, injury or surgery. Both change protein needs in ways a general calculator can't capture — recovery often raises them, liver disease can complicate them. Take the number below to your clinical team rather than acting on it alone.
underweight.title: Your weight is below the healthy range
underweight.body: Your target below is calculated on your current weight, so it is a supportive floor, not a reduction. Nothing in this result asks you to reduce your weight or eat less.
eatingConcern: If food, eating or your weight is a source of worry for you, that's worth talking to someone about — a GP or a registered dietitian is a good place to start.
interp.baseline: Your target reflects the general adult requirement. This is a floor for basic health, not an optimum — most guidelines now regard it as the minimum to avoid losing body protein.
interp.active: You're active enough that your requirement sits above the general adult minimum.
interp.training: You're training in a way that raises protein needs. This target supports muscle maintenance and growth alongside that training.
interp.fatloss: When you're eating less, protein is what protects your muscle while you lose fat. This is the one situation where protein matters most — it is the last thing to cut.
interp.older: From around 65, muscle responds less readily to protein — so the requirement goes up, not down. The old 0.8 g/kg figure was never designed for older adults.
interp.recovery: Recovery and illness raise protein needs, sometimes substantially.
advice.spread: Spread it out. Aim for roughly {{perMeal}} g at each of your {{meals}} meals — your body uses protein better in even portions than in one large evening dose.
advice.spreadOlder: Spread it out, and don't skip breakfast protein. Around {{perMeal}} g per meal works better than one big serving — this matters more with age, not less.
advice.quality: Favour complete sources: eggs, dairy, fish, poultry, lean meat, soy.
advice.plant: On a plant-based diet, combine sources across the day — legumes, soy, grains, nuts and seeds — and lean on soy, tofu, tempeh and seitan, which come closest to complete. Your target has already been adjusted upward for this.
advice.training: Protein does its work alongside resistance training. Without the training stimulus, extra protein has little to build.
advice.hydrate: Higher protein intakes are safe for healthy kidneys, but drink to thirst.
advice.food: As a rough guide: a palm-sized portion of chicken, fish or tofu is about 25–30 g; two eggs about 12 g; a 170 g pot of Greek yoghurt about 17 g; a cup of cooked lentils about 18 g.
crossLink: Protein sits inside the bigger metabolic picture. If you haven't yet, our diabetes risk check and healthy weight tool cover the rest of it.
disclaimer: Lifeline Daily provides health education, not medical advice. This tool applies published population guidelines to the information you entered; it cannot see your bloods, your medications or your medical history. It does not diagnose anything. Always speak to a qualified clinician before making significant changes to your diet, particularly if you have a medical condition. Nothing you entered has been stored.
